cards.front: How do competitive and depolarising neuromuscular blockers differ at the end plate?
cards.back: Competitive blockers occupy the nicotinic receptor without activating it, so ACh cannot open the channel. Depolarising blockers (succinylcholine, decamethonium) activate the receptor like ACh, but they resist acetylcholinesterase and keep the end plate depolarised until it becomes inexcitable.

cards.front: Phase I and phase II depolarising block: how do they differ?
cards.back: Phase I (classical) block: rapid onset, fasciculation then flaccid paralysis, no fade on train-of-four. Phase II (desensitisation) block: slow recovery, fade present, partly reversed by anticholinesterases. Phase II appears with high or infused doses, after fluorinated anaesthetics, or in atypical pseudocholinesterase.

cards.front: How is train-of-four monitoring done, and what does the ratio tell you?
cards.back: Four supramaximal stimuli at 2 Hz are applied to the ulnar nerve and adductor pollicis responses recorded. The TOF ratio is the fourth response divided by the first. Competitive block shows fade, with the ratio falling in proportion to the depth of block; depolarising (phase I) block reduces all four twitches equally, without fade. During recovery from competitive block the ratio climbs back towards 1.0: a ratio above 0.7 usually allows spontaneous breathing, but full clinical recovery needs a ratio above 0.9 (Katzung).

cards.front: Classify: competitive blocker features
cards.text: Competitive blockers bind the {{NM}} receptor at the {{motor end plate}} without any {{intrinsic activity}}; their fade on train-of-four stimulation is reversed by {{anticholinesterases}}.

Competitive: flaccid paralysis; fade on tetanus and train-of-four; post-tetanic potentiation present
Depolarising phase I: fasciculation then flaccid paralysis; no fade
Depolarising phase II looks like competitive block

Phase II: partly reversed by anticholinesterases
Competitive blockers also block prejunctional receptors, causing fade

cards.front: Neostigmine reversal of competitive neuromuscular block: how it works and its limits
cards.back: Neostigmine inhibits cholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at the end plate and overcomes the competitive blocker. KDT dose: 0.5 to 2 mg (30 to 50 µg/kg) IV, given almost routinely after long- and intermediate-acting blockers, preceded by atropine or glycopyrrolate (5 to 10 µg/kg) to block muscarinic effects such as bradycardia, hypotension and bronchospasm. Reversing residual block matters because residual weakness causes hypoventilation and hypoxia in recovery. It does not reverse depolarising (phase I) succinylcholine block; it worsens it. Sugammadex is an alternative for rocuronium.

Competitive: intermediate (vecuronium, atracurium, cisatracurium, rocuronium)

cards.front: Succinylcholine: dose, onset, duration and how it is terminated.
cards.back: IV dose: Katzung gives 0.75 to 1.5 mg/kg (KDT quotes a lower range); fasciculations over the chest and abdomen appear within about 30 s, followed by paralysis lasting about 5 to 10 min. It is hydrolysed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) to succinylmonocholine and then succinic acid and choline, so recovery is spontaneous. Neostigmine does not reverse the block and may worsen it.

cards.front: What happens to succinylcholine in atypical (deficient) pseudocholinesterase?
cards.back: An abnormal genetic variant of plasma cholinesterase hydrolyses succinylcholine poorly. Homozygotes (roughly 1 in 3000) develop prolonged block (phase II) with apnoea lasting hours, which needs continued mechanical ventilation. The dibucaine number identifies the variant: dibucaine inhibits the normal enzyme by about 80% but the abnormal one by only about 20%. Testing is not routine but is indicated with a family history. Mivacurium is also prolonged, but that block can be reversed by neostigmine, unlike succinylcholine paralysis.

cards.front: Sugammadex: what does it bind, how does it reverse block, and what is its advantage?
cards.back: A modified gamma-cyclodextrin that encapsulates (chelates) rocuronium and, less so, vecuronium into an inactive complex excreted unchanged by the kidney, so it should be avoided in severe renal impairment. It does not inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so there are no muscarinic effects. Katzung doses: 2 mg/kg for shallow block (second twitch has returned), 4 mg/kg for deep block, 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal after a single 1.2 mg/kg dose of rocuronium. Adverse effects: altered taste, nausea, hypersensitivity and occasional anaphylaxis (about 0.3% with the 16 mg/kg dose). It can also bind progesterone-based contraceptives, reducing their effect.

cards.front: Classify: neuromuscular blockers by duration
cards.text: Long-acting competitive blockers: {{d-tubocurarine}}, {{pancuronium}}, {{doxacurium}} and {{pipecuronium}}. Intermediate-acting: {{vecuronium}}, {{atracurium}}, {{cisatracurium}} and {{rocuronium}}. Short-acting competitive: {{mivacurium}}. Depolarising (ultrashort): {{succinylcholine}}.

cards.front: Classify: neuromuscular blockers by route of elimination
cards.text: Agents broken down mainly in the {{liver or plasma}} (e.g. {{vecuronium}}, {{atracurium}}, {{mivacurium}}) act briefly, whereas agents excreted mainly by the {{kidney}} (e.g. {{pancuronium}}, {{doxacurium}}) act longer.

cards.front: Why can rocuronium replace succinylcholine for rapid tracheal intubation?
cards.back: Rocuronium is a non-depolarising aminosteroid blocker with the fastest onset in its class, so it is the alternative to succinylcholine for tracheal intubation. It avoids the drawbacks of depolarising block (fasciculations, K+ efflux) and has negligible effects on BP and heart rate, and is used for maintenance as well. Even profound block can be reversed by sugammadex (16 mg/kg reverses a 1.2 mg/kg dose within a few minutes). It depends on liver and biliary elimination, so its action is prolonged in liver disease.

cards.front: Atracurium versus cisatracurium: elimination and side effects.
cards.back: Atracurium undergoes spontaneous Hofmann elimination as well as ester hydrolysis, so its action is not prolonged in hepatic or renal failure. It releases histamine in a dose-related way, causing hypotension. Its breakdown product laudanosine has a long half-life, crosses the blood-brain barrier and at high levels can cause seizures, a concern during long ICU infusions. Cisatracurium, its potent stereoisomer, depends less on hepatic inactivation, forms less laudanosine and is much less likely to release histamine; it is preferred in liver or kidney disease and the elderly and has largely replaced atracurium.

cards.front: Short note: Succinylcholine

points: Depolarising blocker with the quickest onset and shortest action; IV dose 0.75 to 1.5 mg/kg (Katzung)
Paralysis lasts about 5 to 10 min
Hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterase
Tracheal intubation and other brief procedures
Reduction of fractures and dislocations; laryngospasm
Modifying the muscular component of ECT
Fasciculations; postoperative myalgia, more in muscular patients and with doses above 1.5 mg/kg
Bradycardia, then tachycardia and BP rise; arrhythmias

Potassium rises about 0.5 mEq/L; dangerous hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrest in burns, nerve damage or neuromuscular disease, closed head injury and major trauma (extrajunctional receptor proliferation)
Raised intraocular and intragastric pressure; regurgitation risk
Malignant hyperthermia with volatile anaesthetics
Histamine release: listed by KDT, but flushing is mainly a feature of d-tubocurarine, atracurium and mivacurium and is rare with other blockers; true anaphylaxis is rare
Avoid in young children unless essential
Open globe eye injury (otherwise eye surgery is not a contraindication)
Atypical or deficient pseudocholinesterase: prolonged apnoea

cards.front: A patient with kidney and liver disease needs a muscle relaxant for rapid intubation and a smooth reversal. Choose and justify.
cards.back: Rocuronium has a rapid onset among the non-depolarisers and can replace succinylcholine; it avoids the drawbacks of depolarising block and seldom needs reversal, but it is cleared by liver and bile, so its action lasts longer in liver disease. For maintenance, cisatracurium is inactivated mainly by Hofmann elimination (not hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase), so its action is little altered by liver or kidney failure, and it does not release histamine; it is a preferred relaxant in liver or kidney disease. Avoid pancuronium (renal excretion) and avoid succinylcholine where hyperkalaemia is a danger (burns, nerve damage). Reversal after rocuronium or vecuronium can use sugammadex, which encapsulates the blocker, rather than neostigmine; but sugammadex is cleared by the kidney, so in significant renal failure (Katzung: CrCl below 30 mL/min) it is avoided unless essential, and cisatracurium, which seldom needs reversal, becomes the safer maintenance choice.

cards.front: Dantrolene: mechanism of action.
cards.back: It blocks RyR1 calcium-release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle and prevents calcium-induced calcium release. Excitation-contraction coupling fails although the membrane still depolarises, so end-plate transmission is unaffected. Cardiac and smooth muscle channels (RyR2) are only weakly affected. Fast twitch fibres are affected more than slow antigravity fibres.

cards.front: Dantrolene in malignant hyperthermia: why it works, the dose, and what limits its oral use
cards.back: Malignant hyperthermia is persistent calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in genetically susceptible people, triggered by fluorinated anaesthetics and succinylcholine. Dantrolene blocks the RyR1 calcium-release channel, so IV dantrolene is the drug of choice. Dose in the owner's books: 1 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed up to a maximum of 10 mg/kg (KDT, Katzung). Oral use for spasticity is limited because the muscle weakness it causes offsets the benefit, and long-term use causes dose-related hepatotoxicity (a black-box warning).

cards.front: Classify: centrally acting muscle relaxants
cards.text: Centrally acting relaxants include {{baclofen}} (GABA-B agonist), {{tizanidine}} (alpha-2 agonist), {{diazepam}} and {{methocarbamol}}; {{mephenesin}} is no longer used because of gastric irritation and thrombophlebitis.

cards.front: Short note: Malignant hyperthermia

points: Inherited (autosomal dominant) susceptibility, linked to the skeletal muscle RyR1 calcium-release channel and to myopathies such as central core disease
Triggered by fluorinated anaesthetics (halothane, isoflurane), especially with succinylcholine
Persistent calcium release causes contracture, rigidity and heat production
Rising temperature, tachycardia and muscle rigidity
Acidosis and hyperkalaemia develop as the reaction progresses
Usually no signs until an anaesthetic is given
Stop all triggering agents at once
IV dantrolene is the drug of choice: 1 mg/kg, repeated up to 10 mg/kg (KDT, Katzung)
100% oxygen, rapid cooling and correction of acidosis
Identify susceptible patients and avoid triggering agents
Use a non-triggering anaesthetic technique for them

Acts mainly in the spinal cord, reducing release of excitatory transmitters
Depresses mono- and polysynaptic reflexes
Spasticity in multiple sclerosis, ALS, spinal injury and flexor spasms

Abrupt withdrawal (including interruption of intrathecal delivery) can cause hallucinations, tachycardia and seizures

No effect on neuromuscular transmission; drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia (IV)

Diazepam (GABA-A), baclofen (GABA-B agonist), tizanidine (alpha-2 agonist)

Acute painful spasm, backache, torticollis and lumbago

Anxiety with muscle tension; tetanus (IV diazepam); adjunct in ECT and orthopaedic manipulation

cards.front: Why is malignant hyperthermia mainly linked to halothane and suxamethonium?
cards.back: Halothane opens the abnormal RyR1 calcium channel in susceptible muscle, releasing large amounts of Ca2+ and causing sustained contraction and heat. Suxamethonium worsens this. Treatment: dantrolene IV, cooling, bicarbonate and 100% O2.

cards.front: Essay: Centrally acting muscle relaxants

No effect on neuromuscular transmission or muscle fibre
Selectively depress polysynaptic reflexes (baclofen also depresses monosynaptic reflexes)
Mild sedation is common
Mephenesin: historical; gastric irritation and thrombophlebitis rule out use
Carisoprodol, chlorzoxazone, methocarbamol, chlormezanone: efficacy in acute spasm is not well established
Diazepam (GABA-A enhancement); baclofen (GABA-B agonist); tizanidine (alpha-2 agonist)
Baclofen is preferred in multiple sclerosis, spinal injury and ALS
Tizanidine reduces spasticity with less weakness; avoid with clonidine or antihypertensives
Dantrolene acts on muscle rather than the CNS
Acute painful spasm, backache, torticollis and lumbago
Spastic neurological disease; tetanus (diazepam infusion)
Adjuncts in ECT and orthopaedic manipulation
Sedation, dizziness, weakness and gastric upset
Tizanidine: dry mouth, raised liver enzymes; CYP1A2 inhibitors raise its plasma levels
Carisoprodol is metabolised to meprobamate; stopping either after heavy use causes a withdrawal syndrome
Centrally acting: oral or parenteral, CNS depression, no paralysis of voluntary movement
Neuromuscular blockers: IV only, flaccid paralysis, no central effect

cards.front: How do local anaesthetics block the axonal Na+ channel?
cards.back: The unionised base crosses the membrane and re-ionises inside the axon. The cation binds a receptor in the inner pore of the Na+ channel (segment S6 of domain IV), stabilises the inactivated state, and so raises the threshold and stops conduction. Blockade is use-dependent: it builds faster at higher firing frequencies, and higher extracellular Ca2+ reduces it.

cards.front: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity: CNS and cardiovascular features and management
cards.back: CNS: early circumoral numbness, tongue tingling, dizziness, tinnitus; then restlessness, twitching, convulsions, coma and respiratory arrest. Cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, asystole and vascular collapse; bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic. Management: stop injection, secure airway, give oxygen and ventilate, treat convulsions with diazepam or midazolam, support circulation, and give IV lipid emulsion, which has been shown to resuscitate bupivacaine cardiotoxicity.

cards.front: Which form of a local anaesthetic crosses the axon, and which form blocks the Na+ channel?
cards.back: The unionised base is lipid-soluble, so it penetrates the axon; potency tracks the lipid solubility of this base. Inside, the cationic form is the main active species: it binds the open or inactivated channel more avidly than the resting one, prolonging the inactivated state and the refractory period. The pKa sets how much base is available at pH 7.4, which later decides onset.

cards.front: Classify: ester-linked and amide-linked local anaesthetics
cards.text: Ester-linked local anaesthetics include {{procaine}}, {{chloroprocaine}}, {{tetracaine}} and {{benzocaine}}; amide-linked ones include {{lidocaine}}, {{bupivacaine}}, {{prilocaine}} and {{ropivacaine}}.

cards.front: Why does the pKa of a local anaesthetic determine its onset?
cards.back: Only the unionised base crosses the nerve membrane. Lidocaine (pKa about 7.6 to 7.8) has 30 to 40% unionised at pH 7.4, so onset is fast. Bupivacaine, tetracaine and procaine (pKa 8.1 to 8.9) have 15% or less unionised, so onset is slow. Chloroprocaine is an exception: rapid onset despite a high pKa.

cards.front: Ester-linked versus amide-linked local anaesthetics.
cards.back: Ester types (procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterase, act for shorter periods and cause more hypersensitivity; allergy cross-reacts among esters. Amide types (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine) are broken down in the liver, act longer and more intensely, rarely cause allergy, and do not cross-react with esters. Methylparaben preservative is a common allergen.

cards.front: Why is adrenaline added to local anaesthetic solutions, and where should it be avoided?
cards.back: Adrenaline (1 in 50,000 to 1 in 200,000) slows absorption from the injection site: the block lasts longer and is more intense, systemic toxicity falls and the field is less bloody. Classical teaching avoids it in ring blocks of fingers, toes, penis and pinna, where collateral flow is poor; Katzung notes some now question this rule. Use with caution in ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, thyrotoxicosis, and with beta-blockers (unopposed alpha effect) or tricyclic antidepressants.

cards.front: Short note: Mechanism of local anaesthetic action and frequency dependence

points: Binds a receptor inside the voltage-gated Na+ channel (S6 of domain IV); channel pore blocked from the inner mouth
Unionised base crosses the membrane; cationic form (BH+) binds the receptor
Binding stabilises the inactivated state and prolongs refractory period
Greater block at higher stimulation frequency
Calcium increase reduces Na+ channel inactivation and lessens block
Resting potential is unchanged; K+ channels blocked only at high concentration

cards.front: Short note: Why pKa and lipid solubility decide onset and potency of local anaesthetics

points: Low pKa (7.6 to 7.8; lidocaine, mepivacaine) gives 30 to 40% unionised base at pH 7.4, so fast onset
High pKa (8.1 to 8.9; procaine, tetracaine, bupivacaine) gives 15% or less unionised, so slow onset
Chloroprocaine is an exception: fast onset despite pKa 9.1
Potency generally follows lipid solubility of the base form, which penetrates the axon

cards.front: Short note: Differential nerve block and fibre sensitivity

points: Epidural bupivacaine blocks sensory fibres at much lower concentration than motor fibres
Used in labour (mother can push) and postoperative epidural analgesia (early ambulation)
Pain, then temperature, touch, deep pressure; autonomic fibres more susceptible than somatic
Myelinated fibres block earlier than non-myelinated; critical length 2 to 3 nodes of Ranvier
Fibres most sensitive to block are the first blocked and the last to recover

cards.front: Short note: Adrenaline as an adjunct to local anaesthetics

points: Prolongs duration by slowing removal from the site
Enhances intensity of nerve block and reduces systemic absorption and toxicity
Gives a bloodless surgical field
Local oedema, necrosis and delayed wound healing
May raise BP and promote arrhythmia
Ring block of fingers, toes, penis, pinna
Ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, uncontrolled hypertension
Patients on beta-blockers (unopposed alpha effect) or tricyclics (potentiates adrenaline)

cards.front: Short note: Systemic toxicity of local anaesthetics

points: Early: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, dizziness, tinnitus, drowsiness
Later: twitching, convulsions, respiratory arrest; diazepam or midazolam prevents and treats
Bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmia, asystole, vascular collapse at toxic doses
Bupivacaine most cardiotoxic; QTc prolongation; lidocaine has minimal proarrhythmic effect
Rapidly absorbed but slowly metabolised drugs are most toxic
Max safe dose lower in hepatic disease and the elderly

cards.front: Why are ester local anaesthetics more prone to allergy than amide ones?
cards.back: Hypersensitivity is more common with ester-linked LAs, and cross-reactivity is frequent among esters but not with amides. Methylparaben preservatives are often the real cause.

cards.front: Why does propranolol affect lidocaine levels?
cards.back: Propranolol (and probably other beta-blockers) reduces hepatic blood flow, lowering the metabolism of lidocaine and other amide LAs.

Weak base with amphiphilic structure
Hydrophilic amine and lipophilic aromatic ring joined by an ester or amide link
Ester: procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine
Amide: lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine, levobupivacaine
Cocaine is an ester alkaloid, used only for ocular anaesthesia
Reduce Na+ entry during the action potential upstroke; threshold rises
Cationic form binds the inner channel receptor; affinity higher in activated and inactivated states
pKa governs onset; lipid solubility governs potency

Surface, infiltration, field block, nerve block, spinal, epidural and IV regional block

Absorption depends on the site and its blood flow (intercostal faster than sciatic)
Stimulation followed by depression; early numbness, tinnitus and dizziness, then convulsions and coma

Diazepam or midazolam for convulsions
High levels depress automaticity, conduction and contractility, and prolong refractoriness and QTc
Bupivacaine is most cardiotoxic
Hypotension from sympathetic block and direct arteriolar relaxation; collapse at toxic levels
Injection pain; bupivacaine is the most irritant

Hepatic disease and the elderly reduce clearance of amide agents

cards.front: What is EMLA and how is it used?
cards.back: A eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics: lidocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5% form a mixture with a lower melting point, made into a 5% cream that can penetrate keratinised skin. Applied under an occlusive dressing for about 1 hour, it numbs intact skin to about 5 mm, lasting 1 to 2 hours after removal. Used before venepuncture or IV cannulation (especially in children), skin graft harvest and superficial procedures. A prilocaine metabolite can cause methaemoglobinaemia.

cards.front: Classify: relative potency and duration
cards.text: Relative to lidocaine (potency 1), {{bupivacaine}} is about {{4 to 5}} times as potent and {{ropivacaine}} about {{3 to 4}} times; lidocaine has a {{fast}} onset and bupivacaine a {{long}} duration.

cards.front: Classify: special-purpose local anaesthetics
cards.text: The most potent and most toxic local anaesthetic is {{dibucaine}}; the eutectic lidocaine and prilocaine cream anaesthetises {{intact skin}}; {{proparacaine}} is the commonly used ophthalmic surface anaesthetic; {{oxethazaine}} can act on gastric mucosa.

cards.front: Recall: maximum doses of local anaesthetics for nerve block (KDT)
cards.text: Maximum doses for nerve block are about {{300 mg}} for lidocaine, {{150 mg}} for bupivacaine and {{200 mg}} for ropivacaine; the highest peak blood levels follow {{intercostal}} block, so limits are respected most carefully there.

cards.front: Which local anaesthetic is used for surface anaesthesia of the anal canal, and why is it not used for long spinal block?
cards.back: Dibucaine (cinchocaine): the most potent, most toxic and longest-acting local anaesthetic. It is used on less delicate mucous membranes such as the anal canal; its use for long-duration spinal anaesthesia has been abandoned.

cards.front: What reverses bupivacaine cardiotoxicity?
cards.back: Intravenous lipid emulsion, which probably extracts the lipophilic bupivacaine from plasma and cardiac tissue.

cards.front: Why is epidural bupivacaine popular for labour analgesia?
cards.back: At low concentration (0.25%), bupivacaine blocks sensory fibres more readily than motor fibres, giving pain relief with little leg weakness. The mother can push during contractions. In postoperative continuous epidural analgesia, the same separation allows early walking and exercise. Ropivacaine gives a similar sensory-motor separation.

cards.front: Lidocaine versus bupivacaine: how do they compare?
cards.back: Lidocaine: relative potency 1, fast onset, duration about 60 to 120 min, relatively low cardiotoxicity; also used as an antiarrhythmic. Bupivacaine: about 4 to 5 times as potent, slower onset, long duration (about 120 to 360 min), markedly more cardiotoxic, and avoided in IV regional block. Its sensory-selective epidural use at low concentration is its main advantage. Levobupivacaine is less cardiotoxic.

cards.front: Why is cocaine no longer used as a local anaesthetic?
cards.back: Its only classical indication was ocular surface anaesthesia, but it constricts conjunctival vessels and can cloud and even slough the cornea, so even this use is not justified. It blocks reuptake of noradrenaline and adrenaline, causing vasoconstriction, hypertension, tachycardia and mydriasis. It is a powerful CNS stimulant with high abuse potential. It must never be injected, because it is a protoplasmic poison that causes tissue necrosis.

cards.front: Short note: Bupivacaine

points: Lipophilic, long-acting amide; about 4 to 5 times as potent as lidocaine
Slower onset than lidocaine; long duration
Infiltration, nerve block, epidural and spinal anaesthesia
Labour analgesia and postoperative continuous epidural infusion
Peripheral nerve block 0.25 to 0.5%; epidural 0.25 to 0.5%; spinal 0.5% (hyperbaric)
Continuous epidural analgesia 0.125%
Prolongs QTc; can cause ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation and arrest
0.75% epidural in labour has caused deaths; contraindicated
Limits total dose (KDT maximum 150 mg for nerve block); IV lipid emulsion helps in toxicity
Levobupivacaine (S-enantiomer): equally potent, less cardiotoxic, fewer seizures
Ropivacaine: similar duration, less cardiotoxic; blocks sensory fibres more than motor fibres

cards.front: Why is bupivacaine withheld at 0.75% in labour epidurals?
cards.back: Epidural 0.75% bupivacaine in labour caused a few deaths from cardiac arrest, so this concentration is contraindicated. Bupivacaine is more prone to QTc prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias.

cards.front: Short note: Lidocaine: uses, dose-related effects and EMLA

points: Surface, infiltration, nerve block, epidural, spinal and intravenous regional block
2% with adrenaline is the popular dental anaesthetic
Nerve block in about 3 minutes (procaine about 15 minutes)
Also a popular antiarrhythmic (see KDT8 ch39)
Eutectic mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine (1:1) anaesthetises intact skin under occlusion for about 1 h before cannulation
Early: drowsiness, tinnitus, dysphoria; later twitching, convulsions, arrhythmias, coma

cards.front: Short note: Levobupivacaine and ropivacaine: newer amide anaesthetics

points: S(-) enantiomer of bupivacaine; equally potent
Less cardiotoxic and less prone to seizures than racemic bupivacaine
Newer congener, nearly as long acting, less cardiotoxic
Blocks pain (A-delta and C) fibres more completely than motor fibres; continuous epidural use for postoperative and labour pain

cards.front: Short note: Cocaine as a local anaesthetic

points: Good surface anaesthetic; only indication is ocular anaesthesia
Never inject: protoplasmic poison causing necrosis
Powerful CNS stimulant: euphoria, excitement, convulsions, death
Blocks uptake of NA and Adr, causing sympathomimetic effects and potentiating direct agonists
Causes conjunctival vasoconstriction, corneal clouding and sloughing

cards.front: Short note: Surface anaesthetics: tetracaine, proparacaine, benzocaine and oxethazaine

points: Lipid-soluble PABA ester; more potent and more toxic; topical eye, nose and throat only; tracheobronchial spray is absorbed fast, approaching i.v. blood levels

Very poorly soluble: long numbness without systemic toxicity; benzocaine can cause methaemoglobinaemia
Not used for sulphonamide interaction; see KDT8 ch26
Ionises minimally even at low pH, so it works on gastric mucosa; for gastritis and reflux with antacids

cards.front: Choose the local anaesthetic and technique for: labour analgesia, an upper-limb Bier's block, and a dental extraction; state the main hazard in each.
cards.back: Labour: continuous epidural low-concentration bupivacaine (0.125%) or ropivacaine; 0.75% bupivacaine is contraindicated since cardiac arrest has occurred, and bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is treated with IV lipid emulsion. Bier's block: 0.5% lidocaine IV into a tourniquet-isolated limb; the hazard is toxic release if the cuff is deflated early. Dental: lidocaine 2% with adrenaline (1:80,000) for longer action and a bloodless field; avoid adrenaline mixtures in ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis or uncontrolled hypertension, and with beta-blockers or tricyclics.

cards.front: Spinal anaesthesia: injection site, site of action and level of block.
cards.back: The drug is injected into the subarachnoid space at L2-3 or L3-4, below the end of the cord, so it acts mainly on cauda equina nerve roots. Spread depends on dose, volume, specific gravity and posture; hyperbaric (glucose) solutions move to the dependent part. Sympathetic block is about 2 segments higher than the sensory level and motor block about 2 segments lower. The level becomes fixed about 10 min after injection.

cards.front: Why does spinal anaesthesia cause hypotension, and how is it treated?
cards.back: Block of sympathetic fibres dilates veins, so blood pools and venous return falls (limb paralysis adds to this). Treat by raising the foot end and giving a pressor such as ephedrine or mephentermine. Knowing the cause explains why the sympathetic block must be anticipated before the incision.

cards.front: What causes post-spinal headache and how is it reduced?
cards.back: CSF leaks out through the dural puncture. A smaller-bore needle lowers the chance of leakage and so of headache.

cards.front: What is the epidural space and what decides how far the block spreads?
cards.back: It is a space filled with semi-liquid fat that the nerve roots cross. The volume injected governs the spread, which is why the thoracic space (narrow) needs small volumes and the lumbar space needs large ones.

cards.front: Short note: Spinal anaesthesia

points: Subarachnoid injection at L2-3 or L3-4
Hyperbaric (10% glucose) or isobaric solutions; level depends on dose, volume, speed, specific gravity and posture
Lidocaine 1.5 to 5% heavy solution; bupivacaine 0.5% heavy, lasting about 90 to 150 min
Ropivacaine 0.75% for spinal use
Adrenaline prolongs the block
Intrathecal clonidine gives analgesia by itself
Late pregnancy needs less drug, because engorged epidural veins reduce subarachnoid volume
Hypotension from sympathetic block and venous pooling; manage with leg elevation and ephedrine or mephentermine
Headache from CSF leak; less with a fine-bore needle
Transient neurological symptoms (back and leg pain), more common with lidocaine; cauda equina syndrome is very rare
Respiratory failure is rare; intercostal paralysis is usually compensated by the diaphragm
Hypotension, hypovolaemia, bleeding diathesis, raised intracranial pressure
Uncooperative patients, infants, vertebral deformity, sepsis at the site

cards.front: Short note: Epidural and caudal anaesthesia

points: Drug acts mainly on nerve roots in the epidural and subarachnoid spaces
Some drug passes through the foramina, giving paravertebral blocks
Thoracic: narrow space, small volume; thoracic or upper abdominal surgery and catheter analgesia
Lumbar: large volume; lower abdomen, pelvis and legs
Caudal (sacral hiatus): perineal block for vaginal delivery, anorectal and genitourinary surgery
Lidocaine 1 to 2%; bupivacaine 0.25 to 0.5%
Continuous epidural bupivacaine 0.125%; ropivacaine for labour and postoperative pain
Headache and neurological complications less likely
Larger volumes give higher plasma levels
Motor block extends 4 to 5 segments caudal to the sensory level, especially at low concentration
Greatest sensory-motor separation with 0.25% bupivacaine or ropivacaine

cards.front: Short note: Surface anaesthesia

points: Topical application to mucous membranes or abraded skin
Anaesthetises only the superficial layer; motor function preserved
Eye: proparacaine (most used, faster and less irritant than tetracaine), tetracaine
Mouth, throat and airway: lidocaine spray (10% acts in 2 to 5 min for 30 to 45 min), benzocaine
Anal canal: dibucaine, lidocaine, benzocaine
Abraded skin and ulcers: tetracaine, benzocaine, butamben
Intact skin: eutectic lidocaine and prilocaine cream
Stomach and oesophagus: oxethazaine, which ionises very little even in acid
Tetracaine sprayed on the airway is absorbed rapidly; avoid it for bronchoscopy
Phenylephrine adds mucosal vasoconstriction and prolongs topical block
Benzocaine can cause methaemoglobinaemia

cards.front: Bier's block: how is it done and what is the main hazard?
cards.back: Lidocaine 0.5% (20-40 ml) is injected IV into an exsanguinated limb isolated by a tourniquet inflated above arterial BP, and it diffuses back to the nerves. The cuff stays up 15-60 min to avoid ischaemic injury; deflating in under 15 min can let toxic amounts of drug enter the circulation. Safety rests on rapid tissue uptake: only about a quarter of the dose reaches the circulation on release.

cards.front: Compare spinal and epidural anaesthesia: dose, onset, separation of sensory and motor block, and side effects.
cards.back: Spinal: drug goes into the subarachnoid space (L2-3 or L3-4), acts on cauda equina roots, needs a small dose (even less in late pregnancy), and risks hypotension and headache. Epidural: drug acts on roots from the fat-filled space, needs large volumes, bupivacaine is slower and longer than lidocaine, 0.25% bupivacaine or ropivacaine gives sensory block with little motor block, and headache and neurological risk are lower. So epidural suits labour analgesia and continuous postoperative pain relief, while spinal suits quick dense block for lower body surgery.

cards.front: What are the four cardinal features of general anaesthesia?
cards.back: Loss of all sensation, especially pain; unconsciousness with amnesia; immobility with muscle relaxation; and abolition of somatic and autonomic reflexes.

cards.front: What is MAC, and what changes it?
cards.back: MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration that prevents movement in response to a surgical incision in 50% of patients. It is the standard measure of inhalational potency (the lower the MAC, the more potent the agent). It declines progressively beyond about 50 years of age, is lowered by sedative or opioid premedication, and is additive when two agents are combined (for example, 0.5 MAC of nitrous oxide plus 0.5 MAC of isoflurane gives about the effect of 1 MAC isoflurane).

cards.front: Second gas effect and diffusion hypoxia.
cards.back: Second gas effect: a high-concentration gas such as nitrous oxide (70 to 80%) draws in extra gas volume, so a simultaneously given potent agent such as halothane reaches blood faster. Diffusion hypoxia: when nitrous oxide is stopped, its rapid outflow dilutes alveolar oxygen. It is prevented by giving 100% oxygen for a few minutes after stopping nitrous oxide.

cards.front: Describe Guedel's four stages of anaesthesia.
cards.back: Stage I, analgesia: from start of inhalation to loss of consciousness. Stage II, delirium: excitement until regular breathing returns; no stimulus should be given. Stage III, surgical anaesthesia: regular breathing to cessation of spontaneous breathing, with four planes. Stage IV, medullary paralysis: breathing and circulation fail. These stages are blurred in modern practice.

cards.front: Halothane: main adverse effects and why it has declined.
cards.back: It causes dose-related depression of myocardial contractility and a fall in BP, and sensitises the heart to adrenaline, which can cause arrhythmias. It depresses respiration and reduces urine output by lowering GFR. About 20% is metabolised; immune reactions against trifluoroacetylated liver proteins can cause halothane hepatitis (about 1 in 10,000 exposures, about 50% fatal), presenting days after surgery with fever, nausea, rash and eosinophilia. It triggers malignant hyperthermia. Low cost keeps it in use in developing countries, but newer agents have replaced it elsewhere.

cards.front: Classify: inhalational agents by MAC
cards.text: Nitrous oxide has a MAC of about {{105%}} and so cannot produce surgical anaesthesia alone; {{halothane}} has a MAC of about {{0.75%}}, {{isoflurane}} about {{1.2%}} and {{desflurane}} about {{6%}}.

cards.front: Classify: Guedel's stages of anaesthesia
cards.text: Stage I is {{analgesia}}, stage II is {{delirium}}, stage III is {{surgical anaesthesia}} with four planes, and stage IV is {{medullary paralysis}}.

cards.front: Inhalational anaesthetic MAC and recovery numbers
cards.text: The MAC of nitrous oxide is {{105%}}; 1.3 MAC immobilises {{95%}} of subjects; patients wake when the concentration falls to {{0.4 MAC}}.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacokinetics of inhalational anaesthetics

points: Inspired partial pressure drives delivery; brain partial pressure determines depth
Induction and recovery depend on the rate of change of brain partial pressure
Higher inspired concentration gives faster induction
Ventilation speeds the process but does not change the final depth
Alveolar-blood mismatch (as in emphysema) slows both induction and recovery
Most important factor for induction and recovery
Low solubility (nitrous oxide, sevoflurane, desflurane) gives rapid change; ether is slow
Lipophilic agents (halothane, isoflurane) accumulate in fat and slow recovery
Brain and well-perfused tissues take up drug quickly; CO2 speeds this by vasodilatation
Mainly through the lungs; most agents are not metabolised
About 20% of halothane is metabolised in the liver

cards.front: Short note: Isoflurane, desflurane and sevoflurane

points: Introduced 1981; replaced enflurane; routine maintenance agent
BP fall from vasodilatation with preserved cardiac output; dilates coronaries
Pungent, so not used for induction; no seizure tendency; suits neurosurgery
About five times less potent than isoflurane; very low blood and tissue solubility, so very fast
Pungent, irritates the airway and is unsuitable for induction
Needs a heated special vaporiser; fresh, well-hydrated soda lime avoids carbon monoxide
Intermediate properties; non-pungent, so good for induction, including in children
Fast emergence; modest cardiac depression; epileptiform EEG patterns reported
Reacts with soda lime to form compound A, nephrotoxic in rats though no human renal injury is reported; not used in a fully closed circuit; costly
All are non-inflammable
Metabolism is negligible, and renal and hepatic toxicity are rare

cards.front: Short note: Stages and signs of depth of anaesthesia

points: Stage I analgesia; stage II delirium; stage III surgical anaesthesia; stage IV medullary paralysis
Plane 1: roving eyeballs, ending when the eyes become fixed
Plane 2: loss of corneal and laryngeal reflexes
Plane 3: pupil dilates and light reflex is lost
Plane 4: intercostal paralysis and shallow abdominal breathing
Eyelash reflex present with swallowing: stage II not yet reached
No response to pressure on the upper orbital margin: stage III reached
Coughing, tears, BP rise and laryngospasm during incision: light anaesthesia
BP fall with cardiorespiratory depression: deep anaesthesia
Breathing stops, circulation fails, pupils are widely dilated, pulse is thready and muscles are flaccid

cards.front: Short note: MAC as a measure of inhalational potency

points: Lowest alveolar concentration that prevents movement to a painful incision in 50% of people
Stable in young adults; declines with age beyond 50
Premedication with CNS depressants or opioids lowers the MAC needed
Premedication with opioids or neuroleptics potentiates anaesthetics, so less is needed
Steep: 1.3 MAC immobilises 95%; above 1.5 MAC rarely used; 2 to 3 MAC often lethal
Patients wake at about 0.4 MAC

cards.front: Short note: Why blood solubility determines the speed of induction and recovery of inhalational anaesthetics

points: Blood solubility is the most important factor for induction and recovery
Low blood solubility (N2O, sevoflurane, desflurane) gives fast induction
Alveolar ventilation (matters most for high blood solubility agents)
Cerebral blood flow; CO2 inhalation speeds uptake by vasodilating cerebral vessels
Tissue solubility: lipid-rich fat stores high levels of halothane for hours
Elimination is mainly through the lungs; prolonged use of lipid-soluble agents (halothane, isoflurane) causes delayed recovery

cards.front: Short note: Diffusion hypoxia and the second gas effect

points: Rapid N2O uptake concentrates other agents in the lungs, speeding induction of halothane given together
On stopping N2O, it rushes out and dilutes alveolar oxygen; prevent by 100% O2 for a few minutes after stopping
N2O is given at 70 to 80%; other agents are at 0.2 to 4% and cannot dilute alveolar air much

cards.front: Short note: Nitrous oxide: analgesia, uses and limits

points: Non-irritant, non-inflammable, low-potency gas; MAC 105%, so cannot give full anaesthesia alone at 1 atm
Analgesic: 20% gives analgesia comparable to conventional morphine doses
Minimal muscle relaxation; neuromuscular blockers usually needed
Carrier with 0.2 to 2% of a potent agent and 25 to 30% O2 (70% N2O)
Sole agent at 50% with O2 for dental and obstetric analgesia
Expands pneumothorax and air pockets; raises intracranial pressure
Prolonged use: bone marrow depression and peripheral neuropathy (methionine synthase)

cards.front: Short note: Halothane: cardiovascular, malignant hyperthermia and hepatic toxicity

points: Directly depresses myocardial contractility by lowering intracellular Ca2+
Vagal dominance and SA node depression lower heart rate; sensitises heart to adrenaline arrhythmias
Reduces cardiac output with deepening anaesthesia; BP falls 20 to 30 mmHg
Shallow rapid breathing; bronchodilation; preferred in asthma
Hepatitis in rare susceptible patients (1 in 35,000 to 1 in 10,000), after repeated use
Malignant hyperthermia in people with abnormal RyR1; treat with cooling, bicarbonate, 100% O2 and IV dantrolene; suxamethonium worsens it

cards.front: Short note: Isoflurane versus halothane

points: Equally volatile; BP fall of similar size
Isoflurane BP fall is mainly vasodilatation, cardiac output preserved; suits latent or overt myocardial insufficiency
Heart rate rises; does not sensitise heart to adrenaline; dilates coronaries (theoretical coronary steal)
Respiratory depression prominent; potentiates neuromuscular blockers more; pupils do not dilate
Poor for induction (ether-like odour); good maintenance; no seizures; used in neurosurgery

cards.front: Short note: Desflurane and why it suits day-case surgery

points: Fluorinated isoflurane congener; very low blood and tissue solubility, so induction and recovery are very fast
Five times less potent than isoflurane
Pungent; irritates airway with coughing, breath-holding and laryngospasm at induction
Needs a heated special vaporiser
Shortlived cognitive and motor impairment; patients go home within hours

cards.front: Short note: Ether: why it is no longer used

points: Volatile, inflammable, explosive, irritant vapour; very high blood solubility
Potent, good analgesia, marked muscle relaxation by reducing ACh output
Slow, unpleasant induction with salivation and secretions (atropine premedication needed)
Slow recovery with marked nausea and vomiting; competitive blockers reduce to one third
Cheap; open-drop method in peripheral and resource-poor areas, especially in children

cards.front: Justify the rationale of balanced anaesthesia.
cards.back: No single agent gives all components. Nitrous oxide has a MAC of 105%, so it cannot anaesthetise alone at 1 atmosphere, although it gives analgesia. Halothane gives poor analgesia and relaxation, so it is covered with N2O, opioids or neuromuscular blockers. Combining inhaled and IV drugs, each for one purpose, lets each be used at a lower dose with fewer side effects.

cards.front: A child needs face-mask induction and a day-case adult needs fast recovery. Which inhalational agents and why?
cards.back: Child: sevoflurane, non-pungent and low in blood solubility, so induction by mask is smooth and quick. Day-case adult: desflurane, very low blood and tissue solubility, so recovery is fastest, but its pungency causes cough and laryngospasm on induction.

cards.front: Thiopentone: why is its action short, and what are its main risks?
cards.back: It is highly lipid-soluble, so it reaches the brain within one arm-to-brain circulation time (about 15 to 20 s). Redistribution into muscle and fat ends the effect in 6 to 10 min, while slow hepatic metabolism (half-life 8 to 12 h) leaves residual sedation for over 12 h. Risks: apnoea, hypotension, laryngospasm, poor analgesia; contraindicated in porphyria. Extravasation or inadvertent intra-arterial injection causes intense pain, necrosis and gangrene. It must not be mixed with succinylcholine in the same syringe.

cards.front: Propofol: advantages and adverse effects.
cards.back: A 1% emulsion; induction 2 mg/kg IV, maintenance 100 to 200 µg/kg/min. Recovery is fast with little nausea (it has antiemetic activity), so it suits day-case surgery; it is also used in asthmatics. Drawbacks: pain on injection (reduced by lidocaine or an opioid), induction apnoea, dose-related hypotension from vasodilatation and dose-dependent respiratory depression. Prolonged high-dose infusion can cause metabolic acidosis, lipaemia and heart failure (propofol infusion syndrome); unexplained tachycardia during propofol anaesthesia should prompt a check for acidosis.

cards.front: Ketamine: dissociative anaesthesia and when to avoid it.
cards.back: It blocks NMDA receptors, giving dissociative anaesthesia: profound analgesia and amnesia while the eyes stay open and airway reflexes persist. It preserves respiration and dilates bronchi, but raises heart rate, BP, cerebral blood flow and oxygen demand. Emergence delirium and hallucinations are common. Avoid in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and heart failure; it suits hypovolaemic patients and asthmatics. It has traditionally been avoided with raised intracranial pressure, though Katzung notes the cerebral effects may be blunted by keeping CO2 normal. Its S-isomer, esketamine, is given intranasally for depression.

cards.front: Remifentanil: why does its effect end so quickly?
cards.back: It is hydrolysed rapidly by plasma and tissue esterases rather than by the liver or kidney, so its effect fades within about 10 to 15 min even after prolonged infusion. This titratability and quick recovery suit short, intensely painful procedures and infusion techniques. It still causes respiratory depression and can cause chest wall rigidity.

cards.front: Classify: intravenous induction agents
cards.text: {{Thiopentone}} is an ultrashort {{thiobarbiturate}}; {{propofol}} is given as a {{1%}} emulsion; {{etomidate}} is a briefly acting inducing agent with little cardiovascular depression; {{midazolam}} is the water-soluble benzodiazepine.

cards.front: Classify: premedication drugs
cards.text: {{Glycopyrrolate}} is about {{twice}} as potent as atropine with no central effects; {{ondansetron}} is the {{5-HT3}} blocker used as antiemetic of choice; {{ranitidine}} is an H2 blocker that raises gastric pH.

cards.front: Dexmedetomidine: mechanism, advantages and adverse effects
cards.back: The active S-enantiomer of medetomidine, a centrally acting selective alpha-2A agonist (clonidine-like action). Given by IV infusion, it produces sedation and analgesia with little respiratory depression, amnesia or anaesthesia, and blunts the sympathetic response to stress. Uses: sedation of ventilated ICU patients, sedation during endoscopy and regional anaesthesia, and as an adjunct that lowers the dose of inhalational anaesthetic. Rapid hepatic metabolism, half-life 2 to 3 h. Side effects resemble clonidine: hypotension, bradycardia and dry mouth.

cards.front: Which receptors do nitrous oxide and ketamine act on, and how does this differ from volatile agents?
cards.back: Nitrous oxide and ketamine mainly inhibit NMDA glutamate receptors, which gate Ca2+ channels. Volatile agents, barbiturates, propofol and benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A chloride currents; some volatile agents and barbiturates also inhibit neuronal nicotinic channels. General anaesthetics mainly depress synaptic transmission, unlike local anaesthetics, which block axonal conduction.

cards.front: Short note: Preanaesthetic medication

points: Relieve anxiety and ensure smooth induction; produce amnesia
Supplement analgesia and reduce the anaesthetic needed
Reduce secretions and vagal reflexes; prevent vomiting
Reduce gastric acidity and volume to limit damage if aspirated
Diazepam 5 to 10 mg orally; lorazepam 2 mg orally or 0.05 mg/kg IM one hour before
Midazolam: potent, short-acting amnesic, water-soluble
Promethazine 50 mg IM: sedative, antiemetic and anticholinergic
Morphine 10 mg or pethidine 50 to 100 mg IM
Disadvantages: respiratory depression, masked pupillary signs, delayed gastric emptying, biliary spasm, postoperative nausea and urinary retention
Now mostly restricted to patients with preoperative pain
Glycopyrrolate: about twice as potent as atropine, longer acting, no central effects, quick when given IV
Its main use now is to prevent vagal bradycardia and laryngospasm
Hyoscine causes amnesia but delays recovery and can cause emergence delirium
H2 blockers (ranitidine 150 mg, famotidine 20 mg) or PPIs (omeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg) for aspiration risk
Metoclopramide 10 to 20 mg IM; ondansetron 4 to 8 mg IV (5-HT3 blocker, antiemetic of choice)

cards.front: Essay: Intravenous anaesthetics - classification, actions and uses

points: IV agents cause loss of consciousness within one arm-to-brain circulation time
Mainly used for induction; maintenance is usually inhalational, or total IV technique
Thiopentone: ultrashort thiobarbiturate, 3 to 5 mg/kg; largely replaced by propofol
Methohexitone: about 3 times as potent, action 5 to 8 min, more excitement
Propofol: 1% emulsion, rapid recovery, antiemetic
Etomidate: 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, lasts 4 to 8 min, little cardiovascular depression, poor analgesia, myoclonus; inhibits adrenal 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1), suppressing cortisol synthesis
Midazolam, diazepam and lorazepam: sedation and amnesia; poor analgesics
Benzodiazepine effects are reversed by flumazenil
Dissociative anaesthesia via NMDA blockade; raises heart rate, BP and intracranial pressure
Preserves breathing and airway reflexes; useful in asthma and hypovolaemia
Fentanyl: short-acting (30 to 50 min) analgesic adjunct; causes chest wall rigidity
Remifentanil: esterase-metabolised, very short acting
Dexmedetomidine: alpha-2A agonist giving sedation with little respiratory depression; half-life 2 to 3 h
Thiopentone: hypotension, laryngospasm, residual sedation, contraindicated in porphyria
Propofol: induction apnoea, pain on injection, dose-related respiratory depression
Ketamine: avoid in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and raised ICP

cards.front: Essay: Complications of general anaesthesia and drug interactions

points: Risks arise from the drugs and the patient's physiology
Close monitoring and skilled airway management reduce them
Respiratory depression and hypercarbia (more with isoflurane); airway secretions and laryngospasm
Aspiration of acidic gastric contents
Arrhythmia, asystole and hypotension; awareness under light anaesthesia
Excitation and convulsions, mainly with IV agents
Nausea and vomiting; persisting sedation and impaired psychomotor function
Atelectasis and pneumonia after prolonged anaesthesia; mucus plugging
Liver and kidney damage; nerve palsies from faulty positioning; emergence delirium
Cognitive decline, especially in the elderly after long operations
Antihypertensives: BP may fall markedly
Neuroleptics, opioids and clonidine potentiate anaesthetics
Halothane sensitises the heart to adrenaline
Patients on corticosteroids: give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV intraoperatively to prevent adrenal crisis
Diabetics: switch to plain insulin even if on oral agents; insulin requirement rises under anaesthesia
Preanaesthetic assessment and aspiration prophylaxis
Avoid light anaesthesia; assist ventilation when needed

cards.front: What is a train-of-four (TOF) stimulus?
cards.back: Four electrical pulses given to a peripheral nerve at 2 Hz. The TOF ratio is the strength of the fourth twitch divided by the first; fade in the later twitches points to nondepolarising blockade.

cards.front: What is double-burst stimulation?
cards.back: Three pulses at 50 Hz, a 700 ms rest, then the set repeats. It is an alternative pattern for judging neuromuscular transmission beside the TOF; it lets the clinician detect residual block by hand when TOF is hard to judge.

cards.front: What is the posttetanic count (PTC)?
cards.back: A period of 50 Hz tetanic stimulation, a short rest, then single slow stimuli; the number of posttetanic twitches still detectable is the count. The tetanus releases a large ACh burst, which temporarily relieves nondepolarising blockade.

cards.front: Which in vitro preparation is used for neuromuscular blockers in the chick?
cards.back: The innervated biventer cervicis muscle, hung in an organ bath and stimulated through its nerve, with the twitch recorded on a writing lever. Used for suxamethonium and tubocurarine, among others, because the muscle responds to these blockers.

cards.front: Which in vitro rat preparation tests neuromuscular blockers?
cards.back: The rat phrenic nerve-diaphragm preparation: the phrenic nerve is stimulated and the diaphragm twitch is recorded. It is used to evaluate neuromuscular blocking agents.

cards.front: Short note: In vivo assessment of neuromuscular blockade by nerve stimulation

points: Electrical stimulation of a peripheral nerve through the skin
Recording of the evoked twitch of the muscle it supplies
Single twitch, train-of-four (TOF) and tetanic stimulation
Double-burst and posttetanic count as additional patterns
TOF ratio: fourth twitch over first
Fade of twitches with nondepolarising blockers
Posttetanic facilitation and the PTC

cards.front: Essay: In vivo methods for the neuromuscular blocking effect of a test drug

points: Neuromuscular blockers act at the motor end plate; the test asks whether the new drug blocks transmission
Two types to separate: competitive blockers show fade and are reversed by cholinesterase inhibitors; depolarising blockers are augmented, not reversed, by them
Stimulate a peripheral nerve and record the evoked twitch
Use TOF and tetanic stimulation to show fade; add double-burst and PTC to follow the block
d-Tubocurarine and suxamethonium are the agents tested in the chick biventer preparation (Medhi PMECP p171-172)
Anticholinesterases give a different response from d-tubocurarine block in the rat phrenic preparation (Medhi PMECP p169)
Chick biventer cervicis: nerve-stimulated twitch and direct contraction responses to drugs are recorded separately
Rat phrenic nerve-diaphragm: nerve-stimulated diaphragm twitch used to test neuromuscular blockers
The in vivo test shows the whole-body effect of the drug
In vitro preparations give controlled, repeatable first-screen data

cards.front: What does the guinea pig pinch test measure?
cards.back: Whether a forceps pinch still produces a squeak on the drug-treated flank compared with the saline-treated control flank of the same animal. Loss of the squeak means local anaesthesia.

cards.front: What is the corneal reflex test in local anaesthetic screening?
cards.back: A cotton tip touched to the corneoscleral junction of a rabbit eye normally makes the eye close. A local anaesthetic applied to the cornea abolishes this blink.

cards.front: What does the frog foot-withdrawal test check?
cards.back: Procaine 1% is placed over the exposed sciatic nerve in the abdominal cavity for 5 min. The control leg is dipped in saline and the test leg in 0.1 N HCl; withdrawal from the test leg absent while the control leg still withdraws means local anaesthesia.

cards.front: Which drug and form are used in the guinea pig pinch test?
cards.back: Lignocaine 2% gel applied to the test flank; the control flank gets saline or control jelly. Responses are read at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45 and 60 min.

cards.front: Short note: Screening methods for local anaesthetic activity

points: Local anaesthetics stop the large transient rise in Na+ permeability that carries a nerve impulse
Loss of response to a stimulus is the readout
Drug on the test flank, saline or jelly on the control flank
Forceps pinch; absent squeak means anaesthesia
Read at intervals up to 60 min
Sciatic nerve bathed in 1% procaine for 5 min
Dip each leg in saline (control) or 0.1 N HCl (test); no withdrawal on the test leg means block
Cotton tip at the corneoscleral junction
Absent blink after the drug means topical anaesthesia

cards.front: Essay: Screening methods for the evaluation of local anaesthetic activity of a new drug

points: Local anaesthetics block conduction in excitable membranes; at higher concentration they also block K+ channels
A screen needs a readout of lost sensation in an animal or tissue
Topical gel on one flank, saline on the other flank of the same animal
Forceps pinch; loss of the squeak scored at 0 to 60 min
Sciatic nerve bathed in drug; withdrawal to acid as the end point
Test and control legs compared in the same frog
Topical drug on the cornea; blink to cotton-tip touch abolished when anaesthetised
Control side in every animal; lignocaine is the drug used in the guinea pig protocol
Yes or no scored at each time point; compare onset and duration of test and control

cards.front: Short note: Intravenous general anaesthetics

points: Ultrashort barbiturates: thiopentone, methohexitone
Non-barbiturate induction agents: propofol, etomidate
Benzodiazepines: diazepam, lorazepam, midazolam
Dissociative agent: ketamine; opioid adjunct: fentanyl
Loss of consciousness within one arm-to-brain circulation time
Mainly induction agents; maintenance is usually inhalational or total IV
Thiopentone, etomidate and benzodiazepines are poor analgesics, so an opioid or nitrous oxide is added for painful surgery (ketamine is the exception)
Dose-related respiratory depression with most agents (not ketamine), worse with opioids
Propofol: has superseded thiopentone for induction and maintenance, with smooth recovery
Etomidate: when cardiovascular reserve is poor
Ketamine: asthma and hypovolaemia; avoid in hypertension and raised ICP

cards.front: Short note: Propofol

points: Hypnotic induction agent given as a 1% oily emulsion
Enhances GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition
Rapid distribution (t½ 2 to 4 min); elimination t½ about 100 min because of fast metabolism
Induction, maintenance, or total IV anaesthesia with fentanyl
Subanaesthetic ICU sedation of intubated patients (not approved in children)
Suits day-case surgery: less residual impairment, low postoperative nausea
BP falls more than with thiopentone (vasodilatation); HR unchanged or lower
Dose-dependent respiratory depression; pain on injection (reduce with lidocaine)
Prolonged high-dose sedation: metabolic acidosis, lipaemia, heart failure
No airway irritancy or bronchospasm, so preferred in asthma

cards.front: Short note: Ketamine

points: Inhibits NMDA-type excitatory amino acid receptors; not a GABA-A action
Acts on cortex and subcortical areas, not the reticular activating system
Dissociative anaesthesia: profound analgesia, immobility and amnesia
Eyes may stay open and swallowing is kept; limb movements occur
Sympathetic stimulation raises HR, cardiac output and BP
Respiration not depressed; airway reflexes kept; bronchi dilate
Emergence delirium and hallucinations; milder in children
Raises cardiac work and intracranial pressure: avoid in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure and raised ICP
Asthma, hypovolaemia, burn dressings, head and neck surgery, short procedures

cards.front: Etomidate: why choose it, and what are its drawbacks?
cards.back: A short-acting IV induction agent (0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, action 4 to 8 min) with little cardiovascular or respiratory depression, so it suits patients with poor cardiovascular reserve or at risk of hypotension. Drawbacks: motor restlessness and rigidity, pain on injection, nausea and vomiting on recovery, and poor analgesia.

cards.front: Short note: Benzodiazepines as intravenous anaesthetic agents

points: Diazepam: irritant (organic solvent vehicle), so less used now
Lorazepam: about 3 times diazepam potency; slower and less irritant
Midazolam: water soluble, non-irritant, shorter acting, about 3 times diazepam potency
Sedation and amnesia, progressing to unconsciousness with large IV doses
Poor analgesics; reduce central muscle tone but still need neuromuscular blockers for surgical relaxation
Little respiratory or cardiac depression alone; marked depression when opioids are added
Premedication, induction and maintenance adjunct, conscious sedation for endoscopy and angiography, ICU infusion (midazolam)
Action reversed by flumazenil

cards.front: Short note: Fluorinated anaesthetics

points: Isoflurane, desflurane and sevoflurane: the volatile ethers in current use, in which fluorine has replaced chlorine
Apart from nitrous oxide and halothane, every inhaled agent is an ether; fluorine, rather than chlorine, is the halogen used for this group
Enflurane, the earlier fluorinated ether, is no longer used; halothane, the older non-ether, has largely been replaced by these agents
Non-inflammable and non-explosive, so diathermy can be used
Low blood and tissue solubility, so depth changes quickly and recovery is fast; isoflurane is the slowest of the three

All depress myocardial contractility and lower BP in proportion to alveolar concentration; with these three the fall is mainly vasodilatation and cardiac output is relatively preserved, unlike halothane
Metabolism is negligible (desflurane under 0.05%, isoflurane under 2%, sevoflurane 2 to 5%), so liver and kidney toxicity are rare
They potentiate competitive neuromuscular blockers more than halothane does: desflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane
All can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible people
Potency: MAC about 1.2 to 1.4% for isoflurane, 2% for sevoflurane and 6 to 7% for desflurane; desflurane is about five times less potent than isoflurane
Blood solubility: desflurane 0.42, sevoflurane 0.68, isoflurane 1.4, so desflurane is fastest on and off and needs a heated vaporiser
Pungency: isoflurane and desflurane irritate the airway and are poor induction agents; sevoflurane is non-pungent and is used for face-mask induction, including in children
Sevoflurane can produce epileptiform EEG patterns; isoflurane does not provoke seizures, unlike enflurane, and is favoured for neurosurgery
Desflurane suits day-case and prolonged surgery; sevoflurane suits induction and maintenance but is costly and needs a high fresh-gas flow
About 3% of absorbed sevoflurane is metabolised and liberates fluoride, but the amount is safe for kidney and liver at clinical exposure

Sevoflurane reacts with soda lime to form compound A, a vinyl ether that caused proximal tubular necrosis in rats at high concentration; large human studies find no rise in creatinine or BUN, though transient biochemical injury was reported in volunteers
Desflurane is hardly metabolised and is exhaled unchanged, so fluoride release is not an issue with it
Contact with dry CO2 absorbent generates carbon monoxide, most of all with desflurane, so soda lime must be fresh and hydrated

cards.front: Short note: Newer anaesthetic agents

points: Ether, chloroform, trichloroethylene, cyclopropane, methoxyflurane and enflurane are all obsolete; isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane took their place, being non-flammable, faster on and off, and better tolerated
An ideal agent would be pleasant and non-irritant, fast on and off, easy on the heart and liver, potent enough to allow adequate oxygen, and unreactive with soda lime
Isoflurane (1981) displaced enflurane; desflurane and sevoflurane followed with even faster kinetics
Low blood solubility gives rapid induction and recovery, and negligible metabolism means little organ toxicity
Desflurane is used for day-case surgery; sevoflurane is the agent for inhalational induction, especially in children
Propofol has superseded thiopentone: rapid smooth recovery, low postoperative nausea and vomiting, suited to day-case surgery and to total IV anaesthesia with fentanyl
Etomidate is kept for patients with poor cardiovascular reserve because it causes little cardiovascular depression
Remifentanil is hydrolysed by plasma and tissue esterases, so its effect fades in 10 to 15 minutes even after a long infusion; alfentanil and sufentanil are shorter fentanyl analogues
Dexmedetomidine, a central alpha-2A agonist, sedates and relieves pain while barely depressing respiration

Remimazolam is midazolam with an ester link, so plasma esterases end its action; the half-time is very short and context-insensitive, there is no accumulation, elimination is organ-independent, and it is licensed for procedures of 30 minutes or less
Fospropofol, a water-soluble propofol prodrug, avoided the lipid emulsion and injection pain but was withdrawn in the US for slow onset, slow recovery and perianal itching
Methoxycarbonyl-etomidate and carboetomidate keep etomidate's hypnosis with far less adrenocortical suppression

sections.h: Newer relaxants, reversal and local anaesthetics
points: Rocuronium has the most rapid onset of the non-depolarisers and can replace suxamethonium for intubation; cisatracurium releases no histamine and suits liver or kidney disease
Sugammadex, a modified gamma-cyclodextrin, encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium and reverses their block rapidly
Ropivacaine gives a wide separation of sensory from motor block, which suits labour analgesia; ropivacaine and levobupivacaine are less cardiotoxic than bupivacaine
Faster turnover and day-case surgery, better haemodynamic stability and fewer organ-specific toxicities
Cost, pungency, compound A and carbon monoxide formation remain agent-specific limits

cards.front: Newest intravenous agents: what do remimazolam, fospropofol, methoxycarbonyl-etomidate and carboetomidate each change?
cards.back: Each is an older agent rebuilt to lose one drawback. Remimazolam is midazolam carrying an ester link, so plasma esterases end its action quickly and it does not accumulate. Fospropofol is a propofol prodrug that dissolves in water and is split by alkaline phosphatase, so no lipid emulsion is needed. Methoxycarbonyl-etomidate and carboetomidate are etomidate derivatives that keep its hypnosis with far less adrenocortical suppression.
